narrative:
Based on your academic record, the model estimates a 95% chance that you would not pass the bar exam on the first attempt. That is a very high risk, and it is the central reason your law school application was rejected. No personal characteristics such as gender or race played any role in this decision.

The strongest influence on this prediction was your class standing in the third year of law school. You ranked in the bottom decile, while accepted students usually sat near the sixth decile. Being so far below that average strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor, and it told a similar story: you were in the second decile, again far below the accepted-student average of about the sixth decile. Although this factor had less impact than your third-year rank, it still contributed meaningfully to the decision.

Your family income was the second most important factor, though with noticeably less influence than your class rank. As a middle-income student, you were part of a group that made up about a third of accepted applicants, while upper-middle-income families were the most common. This modestly pushed the prediction toward failure, but it was not the primary driver.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your academic performance in your final semesters, particularly your class rank. Building a stronger record, combined with targeted bar exam preparation, would directly reduce the predicted likelihood of failing. You might also consider retaking the LSAT, but your grades and class standing should be your main priority.
